summary: This unit teaches managers to design and deliver a presentation that achieves a purpose. You will learn to set an objective, analyse the audience, structure the content, design slides and present data honestly, prepare and rehearse, deliver with confidence in person and online, handle questions and evaluate the result.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is for supervisors and managers who must put ideas, results and proposals to others: a management team, a board, a parish committee, clients, staff or the public. A **presentation** is a planned talk, usually supported by slides or other visuals, with a purpose, an audience and a time limit. The unit covers planning, structure, slides and data, preparation, delivery, questions and evaluation, for face-to-face and online settings.

A good presentation is not a set of slides read aloud. It is a **plan to change what an audience knows, feels or does**. The slides are only support. This kit follows the order of the work: decide the purpose, know the audience, build the message and structure, design the visuals, prepare and rehearse, deliver, handle questions and then learn from the result.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in your unit
rows: Set the purpose and know the audience
Write a clear objective and adapt content to what each audience knows, needs and worries about.
Research and structure the content
Choose reliable evidence, a few key messages and a clear opening, body and close.
Design slides and present data
Use simple layouts, readable text, suitable charts and honest figures; respect copyright and confidentiality.
Prepare and rehearse
Storyboard, time the talk, check the venue and equipment and plan for failure.
Deliver with confidence
Use voice, body language and notes well; manage nerves; work smoothly in a team.
Handle questions
Prepare for them, repeat them, answer briefly and deal with hostile or unanswerable questions.
Present online
Test the technology, keep people engaged and share the load.
Evaluate and improve
Compare results with the objective, gather feedback, work out simple scores and improve the next talk.

ul: A multiple-choice theory paper with scenarios on planning, slide design, timing, delivery and evaluation, including some simple sums.
A written paper with short answers (terms such as storyboard, key messages, presenter view) and longer answers where you plan a presentation or explain how to handle a situation.
Group practical tasks: designing and delivering a persuasive presentation, and delivering a data briefing and evaluating it.

blocks.note: Several questions ask for a time or percentage sum. Practise the sums in the timing and evaluation sections and check each one twice.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Before you open any software, decide **what you want the audience to know, feel or do** when you finish. A topic ("staff transport") is not an objective. An objective is: "By the end, the management team will approve a J$1,800,000 trial of a staff shuttle for six months." Everything in the presentation must help to achieve it, and anything that does not should be cut.

head: Question
Why it matters
Example
rows: Who are they, and how many?
Sets the style, room and level of formality
A board of seven, or 60 farmers in a hall
What do they already know?
Avoids boring experts or losing beginners
Explain terms for staff; skip basics for specialists
What do they need and care about?
Shows which points to stress
Directors: cost, risk, payback. Staff: what changes in their daily work
What might they doubt or oppose?
Lets you answer objections before they are raised
Cost of the new system; extra work
What must they do afterwards?
Shapes the close and the "ask"
Approve funds; follow a new procedure
What do they need in language and format?
Makes the talk inclusive
Plain language, clear sound, large text, a handout

blocks.p: The same information is presented differently to different audiences. For a new leave system, the **board** wants the business case, figures and risks, briefly. **Frontline staff** want to know what changes for them, how to use it and where to get help.

ul: Use **reliable sources**: your organisation's records, published statistics from public agencies, trade reports and written quotations.
Check that figures are current, and note the **source and date** so they can be shown on the slide.
Collect only what supports the objective. Too much material is the commonest planning mistake.
Check facts twice, especially sums and J$ amounts.

blocks.p: **Key messages** are the few points you want every listener to remember and act on. Most talks work best with **about three**, because people remember a few points better than many. Write them as full sentences first ("Solar panels will cut our electricity bill by a third"). Every slide and story should support one of them.

blocks.note: If you cannot say your talk in one sentence of objective and three sentences of key messages, you are not ready to build slides.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Part
Purpose
Good practice
rows: Opening
Gain attention and show relevance
A relevant fact or question tied to the audience's concerns; state the objective and what will be covered
Body
Develop the key messages with evidence
Each key message in turn: point, evidence, meaning for the audience. Link each to the next.
Close
Make the message stick and call for action
Sum up the key messages, then state clearly what you want done: the **action needed**

ul: **Problem, solution, benefits, cost, the ask:** suits a persuasive talk seeking funds or approval.
**Past, present, future:** suits a progress report or review.
**Compare options:** set out criteria, score each option, recommend one.
**Step by step:** suits training and procedures.

blocks.h: A persuasive presentation to a board

flow: Open with the problem, with a fact that matters to them
Show the cost of doing nothing
Present your solution simply
Give the benefits with costed figures from a reliable source
Deal with risks and likely objections
State the cost, the timeline and the decision you are asking for

blocks.p: The most persuasive evidence for a finance committee is **costed figures from a reliable source**, not general claims. A short **elevator pitch** (a spoken summary brief enough to give in a lift ride) is a useful test of whether your message is clear.

A **storyboard** is a slide-by-slide sketch of the presentation, made on paper before the slides are built. For each slide, write the heading (stating the point), the key visual, and what you will say. Storyboarding fixes the flow and cuts unnecessary slides before time is spent on design.

blocks.h: Timing: work from the slot, not from your slides

blocks.p: Start with the time you are given and subtract everything that is not your talk.

head: Step
Worked example
rows: Time slot
25 minutes
Subtract the chair's introduction and question time
25 − 4 − 6 = 15 minutes of talk
Divide by the number of content slides (average time per slide)
15 ÷ 10 slides = 1.5 minutes per slide
Words at a speaking pace of about 120 to 130 words a minute
15 × 130 = about 1,950 words in your notes at most (script is not needed)
If rehearsal runs over, cut the least important content
A 15-minute talk that takes 22 minutes must lose 7 minutes of content, not be spoken faster

blocks.p: Check: 25 − 4 − 6 = 15; 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5; 15 × 130 = 1,950. **Never fix a long talk by talking faster.** Go back to the objective and keep only what supports it. A rehearsal usually shows that the real time is longer than the planned time, so aim to finish a little early.

blocks.note: A long table or detailed background belongs in a handout, not on a slide. Give a handout at the end, unless people need it to follow the figures.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Rule
Why it helps the audience
rows: One main idea on each slide, with a heading that states the point
People follow the argument at a glance
Key words, not full sentences (for example the 6 by 6 rule of thumb: no more than six lines of about six words)
People listen to you instead of reading ahead; treat the rule as a limit, not a target
Body text about 24 point or larger; headings larger
Readable from the back of the room
Strong contrast: dark text on a plain light background, or light on dark
Easy for everyone, including people with colour-vision differences or tired eyes
Do not rely on colour alone to carry meaning
Colour-blind viewers may miss it; add labels or patterns
One template (slide master) for the whole deck
Headings, fonts and colours stay consistent
Animation and transitions only where they explain a point
Effects can distract and slow the talk
Clear, relevant images
Pictures help memory when they support the message

head: Message
Best chart
rows: A trend over time (monthly visitors over two years)
Line chart
A comparison between categories (sales in five parishes)
Bar or column chart with labelled bars
How a whole is divided into a few parts (a budget in four parts)
Pie chart (only a few slices)
Exact figures people must look up
A short table, or a handout

ul: Start the vertical axis at **zero** for bar charts. A truncated axis makes a small difference look huge and can mislead.
Label axes, units and the time period; show the figure on the bar where possible.
Use **rates** when counts could mislead: complaints per 1,000 visitors, not only the number of complaints.
Show the **source and date**.
Keep to one message per chart. If a table has many rows, highlight the key figures on the slide and put the full table in a handout.
Check each figure twice before presenting.

head: Measure
How to work it out
Worked example
rows: Average (mean)
Total ÷ number of values
Waste collected in four months: 400, 380, 440, 460 tonnes. Total 1,680 ÷ 4 = 420 tonnes
Percentage change
(New − old) ÷ old × 100
From 400 to 460 tonnes: 60 ÷ 400 = 0.15, so a 15% rise
Percentage of a total
Part ÷ whole × 100

blocks.p: Photographs, music, video, text and charts made by others are protected by **copyright law**. Use only material you have created, that your organisation has licensed or that is offered on terms that allow your use, and credit the source where required. Do not use another firm's logo in a way that suggests a link that does not exist.

ul: Add **alternative text** (a short description that a screen reader reads aloud) to every meaningful image and chart.
Use real headings and a logical reading order so software can read the slides in sequence.
Avoid tiny text, low contrast and flashing effects.
Caption or transcribe videos; supply a PDF or a plain handout if the file will be shared.

blocks.note: Remove or cover confidential material before you present to outsiders. Staff salaries from an internal report, personal details of clients and draft figures that are not approved should not be on a slide.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Preparing: rehearsal, venue and back-up plans

ul: Practise **aloud**, with the slides and a **timer**, as you will present.
Present to a colleague and ask for honest comments on clarity, pace and anything confusing.
Record yourself if you can, and listen for filler words, a flat voice or rushing.
Mark pauses and key points in your notes.
Practise the opening and the close until you can say them without notes.

head: Check
Why
rows: Projector or screen, cables and adapters match your laptop
Many talks fail at the first slide
Sound, microphone, lights and screen glare
The back row must see and hear
Seating and where you will stand
You should see everyone, and everyone see you
Power sockets and extension leads, and a plan for a power cut
Outages happen; know what you will do
Internet connection if you need it
Do not depend on it for the core of the talk

blocks.p: Equipment can fail. Protect the presentation with: a copy on a **memory stick** and a copy **online or emailed**; a **PDF** copy that opens on any computer; **printed notes** and a few handouts; and a plan to continue without slides, using your notes and a flipchart or whiteboard. Arrive **early** to test the equipment and to meet people as they come in.

flow: Confirm the date, time, room, audience and equipment with the host
Prepare the slides, notes, handouts and back-ups
Rehearse aloud with a timer, and cut to time
Arrive early and test everything with your own laptop
Check the sound and the view from the back of the room
Start on time with the opening you practised

blocks.note: In some venues a sudden power cut will switch off the projector. A presenter who can carry on with printed notes and a flipchart keeps the audience's trust.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Some nerves are normal and can help energy. The best protection is **thorough preparation**, a rehearsed opening, slow breathing before you start, and arriving early. Speak slowly at the start, when nerves make people rush. Focus on helping the audience, not on being judged.

ul: Vary pace and tone; slow down for key points.
Pause after each key point; silence lets people absorb.
Speak clearly and loudly enough for the back row, using the microphone if there is one.
Avoid filler words ("um", "you know") by pausing instead.
Open posture; stand steadily and move with purpose.
Steady eye contact around the room, not at the screen or the floor.
Natural gestures that match what you say.
Face the audience, not the slides.

blocks.p: Use **brief cue cards or presenter notes with key words**, not a full script. In slide software, **presenter view** shows your notes and the next slide on your own screen only. Reading slides aloud makes the audience wonder why you came.

Agree the order, the time for each person and a **one-line link** to the next speaker ("Now Keisha will show what this costs"). Rehearse the handovers. Stand so that the speaker is clearly the focus, and the others look attentive.

flow: Prepare: list likely and awkward questions and short answers; keep back-up slides
Say at the start when questions will be taken
Listen to the whole question
Repeat or rephrase it so all hear and you check you understood
Answer briefly and honestly, linking to your key messages
Check the person is satisfied and move on

head: Situation
What to do
rows: You do not know the answer
Say so, promise to find out and reply by a set time; then do it
A hostile or angry question
Stay calm; acknowledge the concern; give the facts and the reasons; do not argue or get personal
A long speech from the floor
Thank the person, pick out the question inside it, and answer that
Someone dominates the questions
Offer to talk afterwards and invite others
A question about confidential matters
Explain politely that you cannot share it and offer what you can

blocks.note: **Q&A** is part of the presentation. Plan its time inside the slot, as the timing sums show.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Feature
In person
Online
rows: Reading the audience
Easy: you see faces and reactions
Harder: cameras may be off; attention is easily lost
Technology risk
Projector, sound and power
Internet, microphone, screen sharing and software
Engagement
Movement, eye contact, activities
Polls, chat, short segments, questions every few minutes
Reach
Local
People across the island and abroad, with less travel

ul: **Test the sound and screen sharing** before the start, on the same device you will use.
Log in early; close other programmes and mute notifications.
Face a light source, with a plain background, and put the camera at eye level.
Use short sections and ask questions regularly.
Ask a colleague to **manage the chat** and gather questions, so you can keep your focus.
Have a phone number as a back-up if the link fails, and send the slides in advance.
Tell people if the session is recorded.
Plain language; explain abbreviations and technical terms on first use.
A variety of examples from different groups and places.
Large readable text, good contrast and clear audio; offer a copy of slides in advance.
Check whether anyone needs a seat near the front, a hearing aid loop or a sign-language interpreter.
Respect time, culture and religious holidays when choosing dates.
**Copyright:** use only material you may use, and credit it.
**Data protection:** do not show personal information about staff or clients unless it is needed and they agreed; follow the data protection law and the organisation's policy.
**Confidentiality:** share only approved information with outsiders.
**Honesty:** present data fairly and do not exaggerate; admit uncertainty.
**Respect:** do not use jokes or images that insult any group.

blocks.note: Staff salaries from an internal report must not be shown to outside partners. Remove them and share only data approved for release.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A presentation is judged against its **objective**. Start with the question: did the audience know, feel or do what I wanted?

head: Source of evidence
What it shows
rows: The outcome
Did they approve, ask for changes or refuse, and why?
A short feedback form
Clarity, usefulness, pace, slides and delivery, scored and with comments
Questions asked
Many questions on one point may show it was unclear
Colleagues' honest views
What you could not see yourself
Your own review of a recording or notes
Timing, filler words and body language

head: Measure
Working
Example
rows: Average score
Total of scores ÷ number of people
18 people give scores totalling 81 out of 5 each: 81 ÷ 18 = 4.5
Percentage satisfied
Number satisfied ÷ number who replied × 100
27 of 30 rated it "clear": 27 ÷ 30 = 0.9, so 90%
Response rate
Replies ÷ forms given out × 100
24 forms back from 40 attendees: 24 ÷ 40 = 60%

flow: Compare results with the objective
Collect and add up the feedback
Find the main strengths and weaknesses
Choose two or three improvements
Record them in your notes and apply them to the next presentation

blocks.note: Use feedback to improve the next presentation, not to excuse the last one. One strong comment is not the same as a pattern across many forms.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: write a clear objective and explain how it differs from a topic.
analyse an audience and adapt the same content for different audiences.
choose reliable evidence, with source and date, and a few key messages.
structure a talk with an opening, body and close, including a persuasive structure for a board.
storyboard a presentation before building slides.
work out time per slide, words per talk and how much to cut after rehearsal.
design slides with one idea, short text, readable size and good contrast.
choose a suitable chart, avoid misleading axes and present data honestly.
respect copyright, confidentiality and data protection, and make slides accessible.
rehearse, check the venue and equipment and prepare back-ups.
manage nerves and use voice, body language and notes well.
hand over smoothly in a team presentation.
prepare for and handle questions, including difficult ones and ones I cannot answer.
present well online, with a colleague managing the chat.
evaluate a presentation against its objective and use feedback and simple scores to improve.

terms: Objective
What you want the audience to know, feel or do afterwards.
Audience analysis
Finding out who the listeners are, what they know and what they need.
Key messages
The few points every listener should remember and act on.
Storyboard
A slide-by-slide sketch made on paper before building slides.
Slide master
The template that sets the fonts, colours and layout for all slides.
Presenter view
A screen that shows notes and the next slide to the speaker only.
Alternative text
A short description of an image that a screen reader reads aloud.
6 by 6 rule
A rule of thumb: no more than about six lines of about six words each.
Elevator pitch
A very short spoken summary of an idea.
Rehearsal
A practice run before the real event.
Q&A
The part of a presentation in which the audience asks questions.
Handout
A printed or shared document that gives detail the slides do not.
Copyright
The right that protects an author's original work from copying without permission.
Response rate
The percentage of people who returned a feedback form.

c1.title: A staff shuttle proposal in Negril
c1.text: Mr Dexter Allen, front-office manager at a hotel in Negril, has a slot at the monthly management meeting to propose a staff shuttle that would cost J$1,800,000 for a six-month trial. The slot is 20 minutes: the general manager will take 5 minutes for opening business and 5 minutes are kept for questions. Mr Allen has drafted 8 content slides. The general manager is worried about cost, and the finance manager is worried about whether late arrivals will really fall.

c2.title: Waste collection figures for the councillors, Falmouth
c2.text: Ms Tanya Morgan, an officer at the Falmouth municipal corporation, will brief councillors on waste collection. Tonnes collected were 400 in January, 380 in February, 440 in March and 460 in April. Her first draft has 14 lines of text in a small font on one slide, a 3-D pie chart with nine slices, and a photograph of a collection truck she copied from a website. The councillors range in age, and one has low vision.

c3.title: A town hall meeting in Black River
c3.text: Mr Orlando Gayle, a community development officer, will explain a new drainage project to residents of Black River in a community hall. He plans to read from slides because he is nervous. He has only a laptop on a long cable and no spare copy. Last month the hall had a power cut during a meeting. Residents are worried about disruption to the road, and some are expected to be angry about the length of the works.

c4.title: A video-call pitch from Montego Bay
c4.text: Four staff of a Montego Bay logistics company will pitch to a group of buyers on a video call. Each will speak for five minutes, and a colleague will not speak but is available to help. Some buyers join from countries with different time zones and some have slow connections. The team lead, Ms Karen Palmer, wants the call to start on time and run smoothly.

c5.title: A training day for farmers in Clarendon
c5.text: Mr Leroy Francis, an agricultural extension officer, gave a one-hour talk to 40 farmers in Clarendon about a new way of storing seed. He handed out 40 feedback forms and received 32 back. The 32 forms gave an average score of 4.5 out of 5 for clarity. His slides included a photograph of a named farmer's damaged crop, taken from that farmer's private messages, and a table of figures copied from a company's internal sales report.

questions.q: What should Mr Allen decide before he builds any slides?
o: The colours and fonts to be used on the slides
How many photographs can fit on each slide
What he wants the management team to approve at the end
Which manager is most likely to ask the hardest question
questions.why: The objective drives every later choice. Here it is approval of the J$1,800,000 trial. A talk without an objective becomes a collection of facts.

questions.q: How long can Mr Allen spend on each slide, on average?
o: 1.25 minutes
2.5 minutes
1.5 minutes
1.9 minutes
questions.why: The talk is 20 − 5 − 5 = 10 minutes. 10 ÷ 8 slides = 1.25 minutes, which is 75 seconds. Remember to take off all time that is not his own.

questions.q: At rehearsal the talk takes 13 minutes. What should Mr Allen do?
o: Speak faster and skip the questions at the end
Ask the general manager for 3 more minutes without a reason
Keep all slides and cut the closing summary instead
Remove or shorten the least important content to reach 10 minutes
questions.why: The talk must fit the slot. Cut what does least to support the objective. Speaking fast makes the talk hard to follow, and the close and question time are valuable.

questions.q: Which order suits a talk that asks the managers to fund the trial?
o: Company history, the solution, the supplier list and then thanks
Problem, cost of doing nothing, solution, benefits, costs, the ask
Costs first, then the solution and then a description of the problem
A long list of facts, with the decision left to the audience
questions.why: A persuasive talk builds from the problem the audience cares about to a clear decision. Managers worried about cost and late arrivals need costed benefits and a clear request.

questions.q: What is the average number of tonnes collected per month?
o: 440 tonnes
420 tonnes
1,680 tonnes
410 tonnes
questions.why: Total = 400 + 380 + 440 + 460 = 1,680. The average is 1,680 ÷ 4 = 420 tonnes. Check with the total first.

questions.q: By what percentage did collection rise from January to April?
questions.why: The rise is 460 − 400 = 60 tonnes. 60 ÷ 400 = 0.15, so 15%. Percentage change is divided by the starting figure, not the new one.

questions.q: What should Ms Morgan do with the slide of 14 lines in a small font?
o: Cut it to key points, enlarge the text and use a handout
Reduce the font further so everything stays on one slide
Read all 14 lines aloud so that no one misses any
Add a second slide with the same 14 lines in a larger font
questions.why: Slides should hold a few key words in large text. Detail belongs in a handout or in what the speaker says. Smaller text and reading aloud both lose the audience.

questions.q: Which chart best shows the four monthly totals of tonnes collected, and how should it be drawn?
o: A 3-D pie chart, so that each month looks like a slice
A pie chart with a dark background and no labels on it
A line or column chart, with the axis starting at zero
A table of 14 rows with no chart or key figure shown
questions.why: Monthly totals show a trend, so a line or column chart suits them. The axis should start at zero so a change is not exaggerated, and labels remove guesswork. Pie charts show shares of a whole.

questions.q: What is the best way to prepare for the nerves Mr Gayle feels?
o: Memorise the whole talk word for word and recite it
Avoid eye contact so the residents do not distract him
Leave out the opening and start with questions
Rehearse aloud with a timer and learn the opening well
questions.why: Preparation, a practised opening and a timed rehearsal give confidence. Reading or memorising a full script and avoiding eye contact make delivery stiff and weaken the connection.

questions.q: What is the best plan in case of equipment failure or a power cut?
o: Reading from the screen and waiting for the power to return
A memory stick copy, a PDF and printed notes to carry on
Postponing the meeting if the projector does not work
Using only the slides on his laptop battery and no notes
questions.why: A copy in more than one place, a PDF and printed notes let him continue even when equipment fails. Planning ahead keeps the audience's trust.

questions.q: A resident angrily says the works are taking too long. What should Mr Gayle do?
o: Tell the resident that the question is out of order
Say that the contractor is to blame and move on
Acknowledge the concern calmly and explain the reasons and the dates
Answer in detail and give up the rest of the time to this resident
questions.why: A calm acknowledgement and facts show respect and keep the room with him. Dismissing or arguing escalates the conflict. He should keep the answer brief and link back to key messages.

questions.q: A resident asks the cost per metre of drainage, which Mr Gayle does not know. What should he do?
o: Say he will find out and reply by a set date
Give an estimate so as not to look uninformed
Say the cost is confidential without checking
Ignore the question and take the next one
questions.why: Honesty keeps credibility. Promising to find out, with a date, and then doing it builds trust. A guess may be wrong and become a commitment.

questions.q: What is the most important step before the call starts?
o: Test the sound and screen sharing on the device to be used
Add more animation so that the slides hold attention
Ask each speaker to talk quickly to leave time at the end
Switch off all cameras to save the internet connection
questions.why: Technical failure is the main risk online. Testing sound and screen sharing in advance, on the same device, prevents most problems. Speed and animation make the content harder to follow.

questions.q: Why should the fourth colleague manage the chat?
o: So the speakers do not need to rehearse their parts
So the buyers cannot ask questions during the talks
So questions are gathered without distracting the speaker
So the slides can be changed at the last minute
questions.why: A helper can collect questions, answer simple ones and pass the rest to the speaker, who can concentrate on speaking. This works well in online sessions with many participants.

questions.q: How should the four speakers hand over to each other?
o: Silence while the next speaker finds the right page
An agreed order and a one-line link to the next speaker
Each speaker repeats the company introduction first
No agreed order, so each speaker follows the discussion
questions.why: Agreed order, fixed time and a one-line link make handovers smooth and show that the team is organised. Rehearse them.

questions.q: Some buyers have slow connections. What should Ms Palmer do?
o: Ask the buyers to upgrade their internet connections
Show only video, which uses less data than slides
Cancel the call and send a written report instead
Send the slides in advance and keep the files small
questions.why: Sending the slides in advance and keeping files light lets everyone follow even if the video drops. Planning for the audience's limits is part of audience analysis.

questions.q: What was the response rate for the feedback forms?
questions.why: 32 ÷ 40 = 0.8, so 80%. The response rate is the number returned divided by the number given out. The 4.5 is the average score, not a percentage.

questions.q: Mr Francis wants to know how well his objective was met. What should he compare?
o: The outcome and the feedback with the objective he set
The score with those of unrelated talks by other officers
The length of the talk with the planned length only
The number of slides with the number in his last talk
questions.why: Evaluation measures results against the objective. Did the farmers understand and begin to use the storage method? Feedback, outcomes and follow-up show this.

questions.q: What should he do about the photograph from the farmer's private messages?
o: Keep it, because it is a useful example for farmers
Hide the farmer's name but keep the photograph
Keep it, but credit the farmer in small print
Remove it, unless the farmer has agreed to its use
questions.why: Personal or private material should be used only with the person's permission. Photographs also have copyright owners. The safe course is to remove it or ask for consent.

questions.q: What should he do about the table copied from the company's internal sales report?
o: Keep it, because the figures are accurate and useful
Keep it, but delete the company's name from it
Remove it and use only figures approved for release
Keep it, but tell the farmers it was not meant for them
questions.why: Internal figures are confidential and may not be shared outside the organisation without approval. Using only approved data protects both the company and the presenter.
